newsitem.title: FIJI: Fiji unites to condemn temple desecrations.
newsitem.headline: Fiji unites to condemn temple desecrations.

text.p: Fijian political and religious groups on Thursday criticised the break-in and desecration of two Hindu temples on the racially-divided South Pacific nation.
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said in a statement the attacks during the Hindu religious festival of Diwali were an act of sacrilege and all temples and churches should be respected.
The Fiji Council of Churches said it was saddened by the attacks, which have come as Fiji prepares to draw up a new constitution to replace its current racially-based constitution.
Statues of deities were stolen and smashed at the Soni Samaj temple on Saturday night at Nadi, on the west coast of the main island of Viti Levu, causing F$20,000 (US$15,800) damage.
A number of statues were also smashed at a small community temple at the Suva suburb of Nadera on Monday.
Multi-faith religious group Interfaith Search said the attacks harmed the national spirit and goodwill.
"Fiji is going through a very sensitive and critical stage and we need the people of Fiji to work together hand in hand in nation building," said chairperson Hardayal Singh.
The ethnic Indian-based opposition Fiji Labour Party said it believed those behind the attacks did not want changes to the country's 1990 constitution.
The present constitution was introduced after a 1987 coup, led by then military commander Rabuka, which overthrew an Indian-dominated government.
Under the constitution indigenous Fijians are guaranteed a majority in the 70-seat parliament, but an independent review, sponsored by the government, has called for an end to this system.
The government announced last month that parliament would be suspended for the first five months of next year to allow work on the new constitution.
